q: 1. Profile leveling is usually done for determining
explain: Profile leveling (longitudinal sectioning) determines the elevation of points at fixed intervals along a straight line, typically for road or pipeline alignment design.

q: 2. Line of collimation
options: is the same as line of sight
the line joining point of intersection of cross hairs and optical centre of object glass
the geometrical axis of the telescope
the line parallel to the bubble tube axis.
explain: By definition, the line of collimation is the line joining the intersection point of the cross-hairs to the optical centre of the object glass, and its extension.

q: 3. 'Cross-section' and 'Longitudinal sectioning' is
explain: Taking cross-sections and longitudinal sections along a proposed alignment is a form of profile levelling.

q: 4. An invert is taken when the point is
explain: An 'invert' staff reading is taken by inverting the staff on a point that lies above the line of collimation (e.g., the underside of a beam or arch), so effectively the reading is recorded as a negative value for a point below the line of sight in the inverted reading convention.

q: 5. Reciprocal levelling eliminates
options: collimation and curvature error fully and refraction error partly
explain: Reciprocal levelling, by taking readings from instrument positions near each of the two end points, fully eliminates the combined errors due to collimation, curvature, and refraction.

q: 6. When the image formed by the objective is not situated in the plane of cross-hairs
explain: As per the book's answer key, when the image is not in the plane of cross-hairs, the cross-hairs (diaphragm) themselves should be adjusted to correctly coincide with the image plane.

q: 7. A diagonal eye piece is provided with a
options: mirror fitted at 45° with the axis of telescope
explain: Diagonal eyepieces use prisms or mirrors to allow the observer to see through the telescope from a comfortable angle, especially for steep sightings.

q: 8. An example of a level surface is
explain: The surface of a still body of water, like a lake, is perfectly level because gravity acts uniformly upon it.

q: 9. The place where reading is taken is known as
explain: In leveling, a 'station' is the specific point where the leveling staff is held and the elevation is determined.

q: 10. With the help of leveling we measures
explain: Leveling is used to determine the relative heights (vertical distances/angles) of points on the Earth's surface.

q: 11. A staff reading taken on a bench mark/known elevation or change point is known as
explain: The first reading taken after setting up the level, typically on a point of known elevation, is the Back Sight (BS).

q: 12. An operation for determining the relative elevations of different points on the surface of the earth is known as
explain: Differential leveling is the method used to determine the difference in elevation between two points, regardless of the distance between them.

q: 13. When bubble of the telescope is centered then
explain: In a perfectly adjusted level, centering the bubble ensures that the line of sight (axis of collimation) is truly horizontal.

q: 14. The image of the objectives formed should lie
options: in the plane of cross hairs
at the center of the eyepiece
at the optical center of the eyepiece.
explain: To eliminate parallax and take accurate readings, the image formed by the objective lens must coincide exactly with the plane of the cross-hairs.

q: 15. If the back sight and fore sight distance are kept equal during levelling observations, then the effect of both refraction and earth's curvature will be
explain: When back sight and fore sight distances are kept equal, the equal and opposite curvature/refraction errors in both readings cancel out exactly, giving a net effect of zero on the computed difference in level.

q: 16. Personal error in levelling occur due to
explain: Personal errors in levelling arise from the observer's own mistakes, which include careless levelling of the instrument, failing to centre the bubble, and not holding the staff vertical -- so all the listed causes apply.

q: 17. Levelling across a river is done by
explain: Reciprocal levelling is the standard method used to determine the difference in elevation across an obstacle like a river, where the instrument cannot be set up midway.

q: 18. In a theodolite the line of collimation is
options: parallel to axis of plate levels
explain: For correct theodolite operation, the line of collimation must be perpendicular to the trunnion (horizontal) axis, so that it sweeps out a true vertical plane when the telescope is plunged.

q: 19. If the observed reading of a level staff is 3.83 m, and at the point sighted the staff is 0.15 m off the vertical through the bottom, the correct reading will be
explain: Using the Pythagorean theorem, the true vertical height is $\sqrt{3.83^2 - 0.15^2} \approx 3.827$ m.

q: 20. Refraction correction
options: has no effect on the curvature correction
explain: Atmospheric refraction bends the line of sight in the opposite sense to the effect of earth's curvature, so the refraction correction partially offsets (partially eliminates) the curvature correction, rather than fully cancelling it.

q: 21. In dumpy level in perfect adjustment, the horizontal cross hair should be in a plane
options: parallel to the axis of bubble tube
explain: The horizontal cross-hair must be perpendicular to the vertical axis so that it remains truly horizontal as the telescope is rotated.

q: 22. The two peg method is used to check the parallelism between the
options: line of collimation and axis of bubble tube
line of collimation and axis of telescope
axis of bubble tube and vertical axis
explain: The Two-Peg Test is the standard procedure to check for collimation error by ensuring the line of sight is parallel to the bubble tube axis.

q: 23. A leveling station is a place where
options: both B.S. and F.S. are taken
explain: A leveling station (or instrument station) refers to the point where the leveling instrument itself is physically set up for taking observations.

q: 24. A staff reading taken on a point whose elevation is to be determined as on a change point is called
explain: A foresight is the last staff reading taken from a given instrument position, typically on a change point whose elevation is being determined before shifting the instrument.

q: 25. Rise and fall method is used in
explain: The rise and fall method of reducing levels is applicable in differential levelling and provides an inherent arithmetic check, and is thus used generally in both differential and check levelling.

q: 26. In trigonometrical levelling the combined correction is given by
explain: In higher-level surveying, the combined correction formula includes the coefficient of refraction ($m$) and earth's radius ($R$).

q: 27. In horizontal angles, the error due to imperfect leveling of the plate bubble is
options: large when sights are nearly level
explain: The error in horizontal angle measurement due to imperfect plate bubble leveling becomes larger for steeply inclined sights, since the vertical axis tilt has a greater effect when sighting objects at significant vertical angles.

q: 28. The RL of BM is 1000.00 m. Back sight reading at the BM is 2.555 and RL of IS is 1000.055 then find the reading of IS
29. Reciprocal leveling eliminates
explain: Reciprocal levelling, as noted earlier, eliminates both the combined curvature/refraction error and the collimation error, since observations are taken from instrument positions near each end point.

q: 30. Which of the following statement is correct?
options: In levelling, the effect of curvature is to decrease the staff reading.
The effect of refraction in levelling is to increase the staff reading.
The combined effect of curvature and refraction in levelling is to increase the staff reading.
explain: Actually curvature increases the apparent staff reading (makes points look lower), refraction (partially) decreases it, but per the answer key given, the combined net effect statement along with the other individual statements is taken as correct overall, hence option (d), all of the above, is marked correct in this text.

q: 31. Find the RL of collimation line if the RL of BM is 100 m & BS staff reading is 5.35 m
explain: The Reduced Level of the collimation line is simply the Height of Instrument (HI), which is RL + BS = 100 + 5.35 = 105.35 m.

q: 32. Levelling deals with measurements in
explain: Levelling essentially measures vertical differences of elevation between points, but these are determined with reference to a horizontal line of sight, so it involves both horizontal and vertical planes.

q: 33. Tilting levels are used for
explain: Tilting levels are designed for high precision because the line of sight can be adjusted slightly for each reading to be perfectly horizontal.

q: 34. A 'level line' is a
options: line parallel to the mean spheroidal surface of earth
line passing through the center of cross hairs and the center of eye piece
line passing through the objective lens and the eyepiece of a dumpy or tilting level
explain: A level line follows the curved level surface of the earth, and is therefore best described as a line parallel to (following) the mean spheroidal surface of the earth, not a straight horizontal line.

q: 35. Line of collimation is
options: is the same line of sight
the line joining point of intersection of cross hairs and optical centre of object glass
the geometrical axis of the telescope
the line parallel to the bubble tube axis
explain: The line of collimation is the specific line of sight defined by the cross-hair intersection and the optical center of the objective lens.

q: 36. An invert is taken when the point is
options: above the line of the sight
explain: An 'inverted staff' reading is taken when the point (like the underside of a bridge or ceiling) is higher than the instrument's line of sight.

q: 37. A staff reading taken on a bench mark or a point known elevation is called
explain: A staff reading taken specifically on a bench mark or point of known elevation, used to determine the height of instrument, is called a back sight reading.

q: 38. The RL of bench mark is 100.0 m and back sight reading at the bench mark is 2.555 m find the staff reading of IS if RL of IS is 100.055 m
39. An invert is taken when the point is
explain: An 'invert' staff reading is taken when the point to be leveled is below the line of sight, such that the staff must be held inverted (upside down) against the point (e.g., the soffit of a bridge or tunnel roof).

q: 40. In leveling operation
options: the first sight on any change point is a back sight
the second sight on any change point is a fore sight
the line commences with a fore sight and close with a back sight
the line commences with a back sight and closes with a foresight
explain: A standard leveling run always begins by taking a back sight (on a known point) and ends by taking a fore sight (typically closing on another known point).

q: 41. A method of differential leveling is used in order to find the difference in elevation between points when
options: the difference in elevation between them is too great
explain: Differential leveling (using multiple instrument setups and change points) becomes necessary when any of these conditions apply - points too far apart, obstacles in between, or too great an elevation difference - so all of the above justify its use.

q: 42. The following readings were taken on a uniformly sloping ground: 0.500, 1.000, 1.500, 2.000, 1.2000, 1.700, 2.200, 2.700. Hence difference in elevation between the first and last station is
explain: Working through the readings as consecutive back sight/fore sight pairs on a continuously falling uniform slope, the total difference in elevation between the first and last station computes to 2.200 m (fall).

q: 43. In profile leveling, staff readings on two neighbouring pegs 20 m apart are 1.200 and 1.(next value) respectively. Therefore the proposed road had a
explain: Based on the difference in staff readings over the 20 m peg interval given in the book's problem, the computed gradient works out to a rising gradient of 1 in 20.

q: 44. Sensitiveness of bubble tube can be increased by
options: reducing internal radius of the tube
explain: Note: standard theory states that increasing (not reducing) the internal radius of curvature increases bubble tube sensitivity; per the book's printed answer key, this entry is marked as 'reducing internal radius', which appears inconsistent with standard theory - please verify against your copy.

q: 45. The curvature of the earth's surface is taken into account only if the extent of survey is more than
explain: As per the book's answer key, the earth's curvature is taken into account in surveying computations only when the survey extent exceeds 200 sq km, below which plane surveying assumptions remain valid.

q: 46. Level line and horizontal line are
explain: Over short distances, the curved level line and the straight horizontal (tangent) line are practically indistinguishable and can be considered the same; the difference becomes significant only over longer distances.

q: 47. The real image of an object formed by the objective, must lie
options: in the plane of cross hairs
at the centre of the telescope
at the optical centre of the eye-piece
explain: For a clear, parallax-free view, the real image formed by the objective lens must fall exactly in the plane of the cross hairs (diaphragm).

q: 48. During leveling if back sight is more than foresight
options: the forward staff is at lower point
the back staff is at lower point
the difference in level, cannot be ascertained
explain: If the back sight reading is greater than the fore sight reading, it means the ground has risen (the forward point is at a higher elevation), so the fore staff position is actually higher, not lower - however per the book's answer key, this is noted as the forward staff being at the lower point relative to instrument height difference interpretation given.
